Affiliation:: Brown University (Center for Computation and Visualisation)
Techniques Used: Reduction of quadratic forms over polynomial rings
Data & Platforms: Tables 1.1 and 1.2 (Discriminant data for quadratic and cubic fields)
Application Areas: Distribution biases in modular forms and L-functions
Explicit arithmetic geometry of genus 2 curves
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Trace Formula Bias Analysis: Deriving explicit asymptotic formulas for root number distributions using Petersson and Jacquet-Zagier trace formulas to quantify biases in newform spaces based on level structure and class numbers.

Conic Bundle Minimization: Constructing generic models for genus 2 curves with real multiplication by minimizing conic bundles fibred over P2, thereby simplifying the Mestre conic obstruction to enable explicit Weierstrass equation generation.

Rational Parametrization via Norm Conditions: Establishing bijections between rational genus 2 curves with specific real multiplication and rational points on Hilbert modular surfaces by reducing quadratic forms over polynomial rings to verify vanishing Mestre obstructions.

CM Rationality Field Determination: Proving finiteness conjectures for rationality fields of CM newforms by combining Grössencharacters analysis with Extended Riemann Hypothesis assumptions to explicitly classify quadratic and cubic fields associated with weight 2 forms.
Summary Description: Kimball Martin specializes in analytic and computational number theory, focusing on the distribution of root numbers in modular forms and the explicit arithmetic geometry of genus 2 curves. His work leverages trace formulas to quantify biases in L-function root numbers and employs birational geometry techniques, such as conic bundle minimization, to construct generic models for curves with real multiplication. By integrating SageMath and LMFDB data with theoretical proofs involving Hilbert modular surfaces and CM theory, he provides explicit parametrizations and classifies rationality fields for abelian varieties, significantly advancing the computational understanding of modular form spaces and their geometric counterparts.
